exercises.prompt: Which of these `main` bodies compile? Choose all that apply.

options.label: `let s = String::from("a"); let t = s; println!("{s}{t}");`
options.feedback: Not yet. `let t = s;` moves the String into `t`, so `s` can no longer be used (error E0382).

options.label: `let n = 5; let m = n; println!("{n}{m}");`
options.feedback: Yes. `i32` is `Copy`, so `n` is copied and stays usable.

options.label: `let u = String::from("q"); let w = &u; println!("{u}{w}");`
options.feedback: Yes. `w` only borrows `u`; reading through two names at once is fine.

options.label: `let mut v = vec![1]; let r = &v; v.push(2); println!("{r:?}");`
options.feedback: Not yet. `r` is still used after `push`, which needs a mutable borrow while the shared borrow is alive (error E0502).

options.label: `let mut t = String::new(); let r = &mut t; r.push('x'); println!("{t}");`
options.feedback: Yes. The mutable borrow `r` is last used in `r.push('x')`, so it has ended by the time `t` is printed.

hints: Which types are `Copy`? A String isn't.
A borrow lasts until its last use, not until the end of the block.
exercises.solution: (b) copies an integer, (c) takes a shared borrow alongside the owner, and (e) uses the mutable borrow only before reading the owner again. (a) uses a moved value, and (d) mutates a vector while a shared borrow of it is still going to be used.

hints: `drop(b)` moves `b` into a function that does nothing with it, so it is dropped right there.
`_c` is dropped when its block ends; `_a` when `main` ends.
exercises.solution: `drop(b)` takes ownership of `b` and drops it immediately: `b`. The inner block then ends, dropping `_c`: `c`. Then `end` is printed, and finally `_a` is dropped as `main` returns: `a`. Output: `b c end a`, one per line. Note that `b` is not dropped again at the end of `main`: it was moved.

feedback.message: Not yet. That is the number of characters (`.chars().count()`). `.len()` counts bytes, and `ï` takes two bytes in UTF-8.

hints: `len` on a string counts bytes, not characters.
Characters outside ASCII take more than one byte in UTF-8.
exercises.solution: `len()` returns the length in bytes. n, a, v and e take one byte each and `ï` takes two, so the answer is **6**. `"naïve".chars().count()` would be 5.

hints: The range counts bytes. The first four characters are all ASCII.
exercises.solution: B, o, g, o are one byte each, so bytes 0..4 are exactly `Bogo`. (`&s[0..6]` would panic: byte 6 is in the middle of the two-byte `á`.)

exercises.prompt: You are writing a function that counts the words in some text and returns the count. Which signature is most idiomatic?

options.label: `fn count_words(text: String) -> usize`
options.feedback: Not yet. Taking ownership forces callers to give up (or clone) their string just so you can read it.

options.label: `fn count_words(text: &String) -> usize`
options.feedback: Not yet. This works, but it rejects string literals and slices of other strings; Clippy suggests `&str` instead.

options.label: `fn count_words(text: &str) -> usize`
options.feedback: Yes. It only reads, so it borrows, and `&str` accepts `&String` (through deref coercion), literals and slices.

options.label: `fn count_words(text: &mut str) -> usize`
options.feedback: Not yet. Counting doesn't modify the text, and a mutable borrow would stop callers from reading it at the same time.

hints: Does the function need to keep the text, change it, or just read it?
exercises.solution: The function only reads, so it should borrow, and the most general borrowed text type is `&str`: callers can pass `&my_string`, `"a literal"` or `&line[3..]`. Take `String` by value only when you need to keep it.

exercises.prompt: What does the signature `fn pick<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &str) -> &'a str` promise?

options.label: The result borrows from `x` only, so it may be used as long as `x`'s data lives, whatever happens to `y`.
options.feedback: Yes. Only `x` shares the lifetime `'a` with the result. If the body tried to return `y`, the compiler would reject it (error E0621).

options.label: The function keeps `x` alive for the lifetime `'a`.
options.feedback: Not yet. Lifetime annotations never extend how long anything lives; they only describe relationships for the checker.

options.label: The result may borrow from either `x` or `y`.
options.feedback: Not yet. `y` has a different, anonymous lifetime, so returning it would not match the promised `'a`.

options.label: Both arguments must be string literals with the `'static` lifetime.
options.feedback: Not yet. `'a` is a generic lifetime chosen at each call; any borrowed string works.

hints: Which parameters share the name `'a` with the return type?
exercises.solution: The return type is tied to `'a`, and only `x` has that lifetime, so callers know the result points into `x`'s data and may outlive `y`. The compiler holds the body to that promise: returning `y` gives "explicit lifetime required in the type of `y`". Lifetimes describe; they never prolong.
